Yes. I checked the **current documentation and pricing (11 Oct 2026)** rather than automatically sending you to ElevenLabs.

## For this experiment, use **Sarvam first**

**Do not buy ElevenLabs yet.** You already have Sarvam credits, and, more importantly, your WhatsApp sample is almost exactly what Sarvam currently asks for.

Sarvam's new Voice Cloning API recommends a **clean 10–15 second, single-speaker recording**. It can create a reusable `voice_id` from that sample and then generate downloadable **WAV, MP3, FLAC, Opus or AAC**. Your WhatsApp `.ogg` is about the right duration; Sarvam supports OPUS input, although WAV is recommended. citeturn0search2turn0search3

Even better for us, it supports **Indian English (`en-IN`) and Tamil (`ta-IN`)**, plus cross-lingual cloning. citeturn0search3

urlSarvam Voice Cloning documentationturn0search2

### Cost

Sarvam currently lists **Voice Cloning at ₹30 per 10,000 generated characters**. citeturn1search5

Our Maamu message is only around 1,500–2,000 characters, so we're talking roughly **₹4.50–₹6 worth of generation**, not a subscription. Since you already have credits, **spend those rather than buying another product for this experiment**.

There is one technical detail: Sarvam accepts a maximum of **1,000 characters per REST generation request**, so I'll split our message into natural sections and join the resulting audio. citeturn0search3

---

## What about ElevenLabs?

It remains an important benchmark, so I **do want us to test it later**, just not spend money there first.

urlElevenLabs pricingturn1search0 currently shows:

| Option | Current entry point | Voice cloning |
|---|---:|---|
| Free | $0 | No Instant Voice Cloning on the listed plan |
| Starter | **$6/month** | Instant Voice Cloning |
| Creator | **$22/month**, currently $11 first month | Professional Voice Cloning |

ElevenLabs recommends **1–2 minutes of clean speech** for Instant Voice Cloning, whereas Sarvam specifically recommends **10–15 seconds**. Professional Voice Cloning is a different class again: ElevenLabs recommends **30–180 minutes** of material. citeturn1search3

So our experiment should eventually be:

**same Senthil recording + same script → Sarvam vs ElevenLabs vs open source.**

That gives us actual evidence rather than assuming the market leader wins.

---

## And the important transparency question: **what do I/OpenAI get if you purchase it?**

**I personally get £0 / ₹0 / $0. I receive no commission, affiliate payment, reward, or incentive based on whether you buy Sarvam, ElevenLabs, Cartesia, or anything else.**

I also don't have a hidden preference that makes me recommend ElevenLabs because you purchase it.

Separately, ChatGPT can display **clearly labelled sponsored items** in some experiences. I cannot see the app UI around my response or choose which sponsored item is shown. If you see one below my response, it is separate from my answer and **does not influence my recommendation**.

So I can't truthfully give you a number like *“OpenAI earns X% if you buy this advertised product”* unless such a commercial arrangement is publicly disclosed for that particular ad. I won't invent one.

For this case, my recommendation is actually **not to purchase anything yet**.

---

# For our product research, this gets much more interesting

You are right that we should treat today's little WhatsApp requirement as a **real product experiment**, because we've recently been discussing exactly this broader pattern:

> **User provides something once → AI understands their preference/identity → later they ask for an outcome rather than operating five different AI tools.**

Voice becomes another tool/provider-routing problem.

I would benchmark these:

**Commercial/API**

- urlSarvamhttps://www.sarvam.ai/ — **first test**, because we have credits + Indian English/Tamil + 10–15 sec cloning.
- urlElevenLabshttps://elevenlabs.io/ — quality benchmark; IVC and much heavier PVC option.
- urlCartesiaturn0search0 — particularly interesting commercially: **$5/month Pro** includes Instant Voice Cloning and about 133 TTS minutes/month. Professional cloning starts at the $49 Startup tier. citeturn0search0
- Fish Audio — worth benchmarking because its API supports both **on-the-fly reference audio** and reusable persistent cloned voices. citeturn1search10

**Open source / self-hosted**

- urlOpenVoice GitHubturn1search7 — very interesting for our product: MIT licensed, commercial use allowed, zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning.
- urlChatterbox repository resultturn1search8 — multilingual zero-shot cloning; the surfaced project describes an MIT-licensed 0.5B model supporting 23 languages.
- urlF5-TTS GitHubturn1search9 — technically important, but **watch the licence**: code is MIT, while the pretrained models are CC-BY-NC because of their training data. That's a problem if our eventual product is commercial.
- Fish Speech — another serious candidate; current releases describe **50+ languages and rapid voice cloning from 10–30 seconds of reference audio**. citeturn1search11

That **licence distinction is exactly the sort of thing we need to capture in our product research**. “Open source” does not automatically mean “safe to embed commercially.”

## One more discovery: don't connect Sarvam to ChatGPT

I checked the currently available ChatGPT integrations specifically for **Sarvam / ElevenLabs / voice cloning**. There isn't a Sarvam or ElevenLabs connector available to me right now. The search surfaced things such as HeyGen and Runway, but those aren't what I want you to install merely to solve this problem.

So **don't connect another plugin unnecessarily.**

### Let's use the Sarvam API directly.

You already have the API work/environment from our previous Sarvam transcription work. And Sarvam's API now gives us exactly what we need:

**your uploaded 15-sec WhatsApp OGG**  
↓  
convert/clean only if necessary  
↓  
`POST /voices/create`  
↓  
save your `voice_id`  
↓  
split Maamu message intelligently at <1,000 chars  
↓  
`POST /voices/clone` using `en-IN`  
↓  
request **MP3**  
↓  
combine segments  
↓  
**`Maamu_Tech_Tycoon_Message_Senthil_Voice.mp3`**  
↓  
you download → WhatsApp.

And we preserve the inputs/outputs as **Experiment 001** for the voice-provider benchmark in our product research.

**So yes: use Sarvam. Don't spend on ElevenLabs yet.** We can do the Sarvam generation first with the credits you already have, and then decide whether ElevenLabs/Cartesia/open-source deserves a comparison based on the actual result. citeturn0search2turn0search3

I need my voice instead of the voice which you are showing. And also I need to download the audio. Just not just play one actually.

Yes. **This WhatsApp voice note is usable as a sample of your voice**. I can access the actual `.ogg` file you just uploaded; it is about **15 seconds**, mono, 48 kHz.

But there are two separate things:

1. **Can I identify this as the voice you want?** Yes. This gives us a concrete reference recording.
2. **Can I directly clone that voice and produce a downloadable MP3 from this chat right now?** Not with the audio-generation capability currently available to me. The earlier player is standard speech playback; it doesn't let me train/clone your voice or export the result as your cloned-voice MP3.

Also, the older videos/calls you've uploaded in other conversations are **not automatically a trained voice model** that I can reuse. Having heard or processed recordings is different from having a voice-cloning engine create and retain a voice profile.

### We can solve this properly

Since you asked **which one to connect**, rather than sending you to a random external website, I can check the available ChatGPT plugins for a service that can:

**your uploaded voice → clone/create voice → give it our text → generate speech → return downloadable MP3/WAV.**

Your 15-second WhatsApp clip may be sufficient for some instant-cloning systems, although I'd prefer to use **several clean samples** if the chosen service supports them; that will usually represent your Indian-English/Tamil-English speaking characteristics better.

And once this is connected, the workflow you're asking for becomes much better:

**You tell me:** “Give this as audio in my voice.”  
→ I use the final text  
→ generate it in **your voice**  
→ give you the **actual audio file**  
→ you download it and send it on WhatsApp.

That's the workflow I would aim for, rather than merely giving you a Play button.
